definition: Dogmatic means asserting unproved principles as unquestionable truth — aggressively and arrogantly certain about beliefs no one is allowed to examine.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dogmatic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dogmatic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Coach Benítez is dogmatic about the 4-4-2: formations that win championships elsewhere are, to him, heresies not worth discussing.
Opinionated is weaker than dogmatic: an opinionated uncle has strong views on everything and enjoys the argument, while a dogmatic one hands his views down as settled truths no argument may touch.

Fanatical is stronger than dogmatic: the dogmatic mind still bothers to declare its unproved certainties, while the fanatical one has fused with them — beyond question, beyond proportion, sometimes beyond reason entirely.

Doctrinaire means determined to apply a pet theory to every situation, workable or not — it's about forcing the doctrine into practice. Dogmatic is about the manner of belief itself: laying down unproved principles as truths no one may question.
Inflexible means unwilling to bend — about plans, rules, or schedules of any kind. Dogmatic is inflexibility about beliefs specifically, delivered with the arrogance of total certainty.

Over thirty years on the forum, the astronomy club's founder grew dogmatic: any photograph that contradicted his pet theory was waved off as 'amateur error,' and when new members asked what evidence supported the theory itself, he replied that some things are simply understood.
Notice what's missing: proof, and any willingness to be questioned.
He doesn't argue for his belief — he hands it down as settled truth and treats the question itself as the offense.
That arrogant certainty about an unproved principle is exactly what dogmatic condemns.
Dogmatic condemns the manner, not the belief: a person can be right and still dogmatic if they proclaim rather than prove.
Confident and firm can be compliments; dogmatic never is — it adds arrogance and the refusal to be questioned.
Its parent noun dogma stays neutral in religion, where it names official doctrine, but turns pejorative almost everywhere else.

For thirty years, students at the medical college learned Professor Harlan's first rule: disease travels in bad air, and nowhere else.
The rule was not offered as a theory.
It was dogmatic bedrock — printed in his syllabus as 'settled beyond dispute,' with a warning that questions about it wasted the class's time.
When a young instructor presented water-pump data from a cholera outbreak, Harlan did not examine the charts; he canceled the seminar.
No proof of the rule was ever given, one student wrote later.
Proof was for hypotheses, and the professor did not deal in hypotheses.
The college's map of the outbreak, drawn by that instructor, now hangs where the syllabus used to.
